https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141381.text: Poland urges EU to fine Meta €250 M over scam ads and false advertising Polish authorities report Meta failed to act on most flagged fraudulent ads, escalating pressure for strict EU penalties against online scams With that stern warning, Poland is officially taking the fight against online fraud to Brussels, demanding a massive €250 million penalty against Meta. Behind the push is a shocking cybersecurity audit revealing that tech giants are routinely turning a blind eye to dangerous financial scams—leaving millions of users vulnerable to predatory online ads. Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski formally asked the European Commission to impose a $291 million fine on Meta, declaring that platform inaction on fraudulent promotions has gone too far. Data from CERT Polska Poland’s national cybersecurity incident response team revealed that out of 122 flagged fraudulent ads, Meta refused to remove them in 86.8% of the cases (106 instances), removing only 10. In a letter to the European Commission that tests conducted by CERT Polska, the national cybersecurity incident response team, found 122 advertisements that were classified as fraudulent. "In 106 cases, or 86.8% of reports, Meta concluded the case with a decision not to remove the advertisement. Only 10 ads were removed, and in 6 cases no response was provided," minister Krzysztof Gawkowski posted on X. "I also call on Meta to immediately introduce effective tools to eliminate scams, false advertising, and the promotion of illegal applications," he added. As reported by Reuters, Meta platform came under fire for allegations that its products were harmful to children and that the company was misleading the public about their safety. In Poland, the platform was criticized for failing to effectively respond to fraudulent advertisements and sued by billionaire Rafal Brzoska over fake advertisements. The move intensifies Europe-wide compliance scrutiny on Big Tech under EU digital frameworks, compounding pressure on Meta regarding content oversight and user safety. In lawsuit filed by Brzoska, the Warsaw appellate court ruled in April 2026 that Meta was responsible for adds it hosts on its platforms. In court Mark Zuckerberg founded platform has argued it is not responsible for the fraudulent actions of its users. "Despite repeated reports from the relevant Polish authorities and teams responsible for cybersecurity, Meta still does not provide an effective and adequate response ​to fraudulent advertisements," minister Krzysztof Gawkowski posted on X. https://www.breitbart.com/europe/2026/09.text: Boris Johnson was reportedly forced to evacuate from his train travelling from Ukraine to Poland after the rail line was struck in a Russian drone strike. According to reports, Mr Johnson was returning from the YES international security conference in Kyiv when he and others were woken up on their train at around 5am local time on Sunday morning by guards after another train was struck on the line ahead near Volyn, near the Polish border. London’s Daily Telegraph reported that the former prime minister was unharmed and that there were no casualties as a result of the attack. Johnson has long stood as one of Ukraine’s top international allies, with the British politician taking an early hawkish stance towards the Russian invasion, including by sending British anti-tank weapons and billions in aid to Ukraine during his time in office. His staunch support for the Ukrainian war effort won Johnson many admirers in Ukraine, with the former UK leader even having pastries named after him in Kyiv. A poll published in June of 2022 found that he was the most popular foreign leader in Ukraine, with a 90 per cent approval rating, putting Johnson on par with Zelensky at the time. In addition to the former UK prime minister, the train was also carrying diplomats and politicians from other European nations, including former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt and German Green MP Robin Wagener, who told Der Spiegel : “These drone attacks are blind terror against Ukrainian civilians and a dangerous escalation in Putin’s war.” “Russia is becoming more and more unscrupulous and is setting fires right on the border with the European Union and NATO. We must finally set clear limits to this terror,” Wagner added. The apparent Russian drone strike also reportedly caused alarm across the border, with Polish Air Force fighter jets being scrambled in case drones entered their territory. Earlier this week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia may soon intensify attacks near European borders in Ukraine in the coming weeks. “Russia already decided to engage in provocative attacks on border crossing points, for example in Moldova,” he said on Thursday. “We expect similar actions regarding border crossings with Ukraine in other countries as well, including Poland.” Follow Kurt Zindulka on X: Follow @KurtZindulka or e-mail to: kzindulka@breitbart.com COMMENTS Please let us know if you're having issues with commenting. https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text: Rohingya refugees at their camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, react during a live broadcast of the international court of justice Myanmar genocide ruling. Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA View image in fullscreen Rohingya refugees at their camp in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, react during a live broadcast of the international court of justice Myanmar genocide ruling. Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA Global development ‘Everyone struggled for this justice’: tears in court as Rohingya vindicated in Myanmar genocide ruling Relief in the immediate aftermath of a landmark ruling, but what happens next is in the hands of governments around the world Supported by About this content Kaamil Ahmed in The Hague and Yassin Abdumonab in Cox's Bazar Thu 19 Nov 2026 11.15 EST Last modified on Fri 20 Nov 2026 00.21 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google There were tears in the halls of The Hague in the Netherlands and an eruption of applause in the refugee camps of Bangladesh as the scattered communities of Rohingya watched the UN’s top court rule the Myanmar military had committed genocide against them. For almost a decade, the Rohingya have awaited this moment; recognition from the international court of justice (ICJ) that Myanmar in 2017 intentionally tried to destroy the mostly Muslim minority group through a campaign of mass killings and rape. More than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to neighbouring Bangladesh . By the time they spilled into the court’s halls, the relief was evident. A Rohingya community leader threw a big thumbs up as he left the courtroom and others immediately took out their phones to call family in the refugee camps. Salma, 30, a Rohingya survivor who lost family members in the 2017 genocide, said: “Everyone worked hard and struggled for this justice, for this cause. When they hear it today, everyone will be happy, thank God. I don’t know how to express it or even what to do with myself.” View image in fullscreen The Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow, centre, speaking at the ICJ in The Hague on Thursday: ‘The victory belongs to the Rohingya. They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe.’ Photograph: Jeroen Jumelet/ANP/AFP/Getty Images Another Rohingya present, who cannot be named because of safety concerns, said they cried as the judge went through each of the rulings. “During the last few minutes I couldn’t even sit down any more, I had to move to the back because I didn’t know how I’d react,” they said. “I saw some of the other Rohingya around me crying. They were so emotional. “Now the responsibility is with the international governments. It has been declared genocide now and they have to act.” In Bangladesh, where most of the Rohingya population have lived – in the world’s largest refugee camp – since being forced to flee in 2017, the verdict was translated into the Rohingya language for the crowds who had gathered to watch on screens specially set up for the purpose. They immediately leapt up, cheering, applauding and shouting gratitude for the Gambia – the faraway African nation that brought the case to the ICJ on behalf of the stateless minority. Many held posters that read “Thank You Gambia” and “Justice = Safe Return”. “Since we arrived here, we have been waiting and looking forward to this justice,” said Farida Khatun, 50, who has been a refugee in Bangladesh since 2017, when her village, Tula Toli, was targeted by soldiers. The village in north-western Myanmar, near the Bangladesh border, was the scene of a massacre in August of that year, with reports of mass killings and gang rapes . She said, however, that she does not expect to be able to return home. Tula Toli was completely destroyed by Myanmar’s forces and no longer exists. “Even though today’s verdict makes us happy, my heart still cannot believe that they will take us back in true peace.” The case has taken seven years to reach this point, with Rohingya researchers working to collect testimony from survivors. The initial hope for justice had faded during the long wait for a ruling. Many were also left deflated during early hearings when the one-time pro-democracy hero Aung San Suu Kyi defended the Myanmar military at The Hague. View image in fullscreen Yusuf Ali, a Rohingya justice campaigner, outside the ICJ in The Hague on the day of the ruling. Photograph: Kaamil Ahmed/The Guardian Before today’s ruling, some were optimistic, others were prepared to be disappointed, but all said they knew themselves that they were victims of genocide. The tension was finally released when the court declared Myanmar was responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, highlighting the use of sexual violence and attacks on children alongside the killing of Rohingya who tried to flee violence, which it said meant the violence amounted to more than ethnic cleansing. The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations for the Rohingya and end continuing breaches of the genocide convention. View image in fullscreen Rohingya refugees in Cox’s Bazar thank the Gambia for its role as they watch a live broadcast of the ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling. Photograph: Yassin Abdumonab/EPA There is now also an international criminal court investigation into the violence of 2017, looking specifically at the crime of mass deportation, and for which prosecutors in 2024 sought an arrest warrant for Myanmar’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing. With continuing violence against the Rohingya , the possibility of a return to Myanmar, as happened after previous exoduses to Bangladesh in 1978 and the early 1990s, remains unlikely. But many hope the ICJ ruling will be the start of a process of ensuring justice and lead to real international pressure to ensure their safety in Myanmar. “We will be able to return to our homeland – with our rights, with our citizenship, and having received our full security. We will be able to return,” says Salma.
